chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Malik ibn Attiyah from Abu Hamzah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The son of al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah died, so Umm Salama said to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family): 'The family of al-Mughirah have established a mourning period (manahah), so I will go to them.' He gave her permission, so she put on her clothes and prepared herself. She was so beautiful that she was like a jinn. When she stood and let down her hair, it covered her body, and the end of it was tied with her anklet. She summoned her cousin to stand before the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and said: 'I announce the death of al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Abu al-Walid, the youth of the clan, the protector of the truth, the noble one, who ascends in seeking the single one (or the unique one). He was indeed a rain (abundant blessing) in the years, and Ja'far a downpour and a provision.' The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did not object to her regarding that, nor did he say anything.

key_terms.أَنْعَى: To announce or proclaim the death (elegy)
key_terms.أُمُّ سَلَمَةَ: Umm Salama, a prominent wife of the Prophet
key_terms.الْوَلِيدُ بْنُ الْوَلِيدِ: Al-Walid ibn al-Walid, a companion of the Prophet
key_terms.جَانٌّ: Jinn, often used in classical Arabic to describe striking beauty or ethereal presence
key_terms.جَعْفَرًا: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, often mentioned alongside al-Walid in this context
key_terms.فَمَا عَابَ عَلَيْهَا: He did not object or criticize her
key_terms.مَنَاحَةً: A period of established mourning or lamentation

ai.seo_question: What did Umm Salama do when the family of al-Mughirah established a mourning period, and how did the Prophet react?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the pre-Islamic and early Islamic custom of *manahah* (public mourning processions), where women would recite elegies to honor the deceased's virtues. The Prophet’s (peace be upon him and his family) silence in response to Umm Salama’s poetic eulogy of al-Walid ibn al-Walid signifies his approval of this practice, validating the use of poetry for commemoration within the Shia jurisprudential tradition. It serves as a key evidence for the permissibility of women participating in public mourning rituals and reciting poetry that highlights the deceased's social and moral qualities.
